title: qXR flags suspicious nodules on chest X-rays taken for non-respiratory reasons; five adults without respiratory symptoms diagnosed with early-stage lung cancer
summary: Qure.ai's qXR flagged lung nodules on chest X-rays taken for other reasons; computed tomography and biopsy confirmed early-stage lung cancer in five adults, and four had surgery.
account: CREATE (NCT05817110) was a prospective multicenter study. The deep-learning software qXR (Qure.ai) was adopted for routine use on all chest X-rays across participating centers from April 2023 to December 2024. The parent study's main paper was published on 19 January 2026 by authors who include AstraZeneca and Qure.ai staff. It states that a site radiologist confirmed each qXR flag before enrollment. A case series in Cureus in March 2026 describes five individuals found through the AI pathway, none with respiratory symptoms. The case series names neither the centers nor their cities. Its clinical authors are at Hacettepe University (Ankara, Turkey) and with Aarthi Scans and Sri Ramachandra Medical College and Hospital (Chennai, India). In each case, qXR flagged suspicious pulmonary nodules on X-rays taken for non-respiratory reasons. The patients were a 57-year-old man screened before anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) therapy for ulcerative colitis, a 64-year-old man with fever, a 65-year-old woman at a smoking-cessation consultation, and two men aged 35 and 75 at annual health checks. In all five cases the reviewing radiologist or pulmonologist agreed with the AI finding. Computed tomography (CT) and biopsy confirmed early-stage lung cancer in all five. Four underwent curative surgery, two with adjuvant chemotherapy, and one chose chemotherapy alone. The case series does not state whether the original X-ray reports noted the nodules. The trial registry, updated on 19 August 2026, lists the study as active, with completion expected on 6 December 2026.
purpose: qXR is built to detect abnormalities including pulmonary nodules on chest X-rays. Flagging incidental nodules is its intended function.
deployer: Participating centers of the CREATE study, not named in the paper; the clinical authors are affiliated with Hacettepe University (Ankara) and with Aarthi Scans and Sri Ramachandra Medical College and Hospital (Chennai)
segment: AI on routine chest X-rays in a multicentre study

ratings.reason: Five adults without respiratory symptoms had early-stage lung cancer diagnosed, four with curative surgery. The authors report positive outcomes but no survival data.

ai_role.statement: qXR flagged a nodule on each X-ray ordered for an unrelated reason. A radiologist or pulmonologist then reviewed the flag, agreed with it and recommended low-dose CT, with or without PET-CT; biopsy followed. The report does not say whether radiologists had reported the nodules before the flag. The AI's contribution thus rests on the authors' judgment that the cases would otherwise have been missed or delayed. One of ten authors is a Qure.ai employee and the study was funded by AstraZeneca.

fields.summary: Qure.ai's qXR flagged lung nodules on chest X-rays taken for other reasons; computed tomography and biopsy confirmed early-stage lung cancer in five adults, and four had surgery.
fields.account: CREATE (NCT05817110) was a prospective multicenter study. The deep-learning software qXR (Qure.ai) was adopted for routine use on all chest X-rays across participating centers from April 2023 to December 2024. The parent study's main paper was published on 19 January 2026 by authors who include AstraZeneca and Qure.ai staff. It states that a site radiologist confirmed each qXR flag before enrollment. A case series in Cureus in March 2026 describes five individuals found through the AI pathway, none with respiratory symptoms. The case series names neither the centers nor their cities. Its clinical authors are at Hacettepe University (Ankara, Turkey) and with Aarthi Scans and Sri Ramachandra Medical College and Hospital (Chennai, India). In each case, qXR flagged suspicious pulmonary nodules on X-rays taken for non-respiratory reasons. The patients were a 57-year-old man screened before anti-tumor necrosis factor (anti-TNF) therapy for ulcerative colitis, a 64-year-old man with fever, a 65-year-old woman at a smoking-cessation consultation, and two men aged 35 and 75 at annual health checks. In all five cases the reviewing radiologist or pulmonologist agreed with the AI finding. Computed tomography (CT) and biopsy confirmed early-stage lung cancer in all five. Four underwent curative surgery, two with adjuvant chemotherapy, and one chose chemotherapy alone. The case series does not state whether the original X-ray reports noted the nodules. The trial registry, updated on 19 August 2026, lists the study as active, with completion expected on 6 December 2026.

echoes.setting: Yongin Severance Hospital, South Korea: a different commercial AI product (Lunit INSIGHT CXR) read all chest radiographs from March 2020; from March 2020 to February 2022, 13 of 75 resectable lung cancers were found incidentally, all flagged as nodules by the software (Kwak et al., PLoS One, 10 March 2023)

Same Korean hospital, March 2021 to February 2022: about 1% of 14,563 patients outside pulmonology had unexpected AI-detected lung nodules, and most of those with follow-up were true positives (Hwang et al., Scientific Reports, 13 November 2023)
